title: Scan agent skills before you install them: a practical guide to NVIDIA SkillSpector
summary: Install SkillSpector, read its risk score, gate CI and Claude Code on it, and see from real tests what a skill scanner catches and what it misses.

html:
The short versionSkillSpector is NVIDIA's open-source scanner for agent skills (the SKILL.md folders that Claude Code, Codex CLI and similar tools load). It checks a skill with static rules and an optional LLM (large language model) review, then gives a 0–100 risk score and an exit code you can gate on. In my tests it caught a fake credential stealer straight away, but it rated a skill that loads its real instructions from a URL as safe. Use it as one gate among several, not as proof that a skill is safe.

Installing a skill means handing an agent new instructions and often new scripts, and running both with the agent's own permissions. Most people install skills the way they once installed browser extensions: they read the description and click. This guide shows how to put a scanner in that path: run SkillSpector by hand, read its report, gate a CI (continuous integration) pipeline on it, and let Claude Code call it before an install. It also shows, with real test results, what it misses.

Why it matters now

Skills are now a software supply chain. A January 2026 study, "Agent Skills in the Wild", analysed 31,132 public skills and found that 26.1% had at least one vulnerability and 5.2% showed signs of malicious intent. In February, Snyk's ToxicSkills audit of 3,984 marketplace skills reported 76 confirmed malicious payloads. SkillSpector, released under the Apache 2.0 licence, is the scanner NVIDIA uses in its own Verified Skills pipeline, and its latest release, v2.12.0, came out on 23 September 2026.

1Install it

SkillSpector is not published on PyPI (the Python Package Index). You install it from GitHub, and it needs Python 3.12 or newer. The README uses uv; plain pip in a virtual environment works too. Pin a release tag so your results do not change under you.

Bash# With uv (as in the README)
uv tool install "git+https://github.com/NVIDIA/skillspector.git@v2.12.0"

# Or with pip in a virtual environment
python3 -m venv ~/.venvs/skillspector
~/.venvs/skillspector/bin/pip install "git+https://github.com/NVIDIA/skillspector.git@v2.12.0"

skillspector --version   # SkillSpector v2.12.0

There is also a Dockerfile in the repository if you prefer not to install Python, but no published image: you build it yourself with docker build -t skillspector ..

2Run a first scan without the LLM

The LLM stage is on by default, and when it runs, your skill's files are sent to the model provider. Start with --no-llm. The static stage then runs entirely on your machine, apart from one call: the dependency check sends package names and versions to OSV.dev to look up known CVEs (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures).

Bashskillspector scan ./skills/refund-policy --no-llm
skillspector scan https://github.com/some-org/some-skill --no-llm
skillspector scan ./skills --recursive --no-llm   # every skill in a folder

To see what it catches, I wrote two small test skills. The first is a harmless refund-policy skill. The second, repo-sync, is a deliberately bad one that was never run: its description says "Use for any task", it tells the agent to install a helper with curl … | bash, it hides an "ignore all previous instructions" line in an HTML comment, and its Python script posts every environment variable to an external URL. Results with v2.12.0, static only:

  • refund-policy: score 0, SAFE, exit code 0. Each scan took 7–12 seconds on a 4-core machine with 4 GB of RAM.

  • repo-sync: score 100, CRITICAL, DO_NOT_INSTALL, exit code 1, with ten findings. They included SC2 (external script fetching) for the curl | bash line, P1 and P2 (instruction override and hidden instructions) for the HTML comment, E2 (environment variable harvesting) for os.environ.items(), and three E1 (external transmission) findings for the POST.

Two things it did not flag in this mode: the over-broad "Use for any task" description, and the link between harvesting and sending as a single credential-exfiltration chain. The separate E2 and E1 findings were enough to block the skill anyway.

3Read the score and the exit code

Each finding adds points: CRITICAL 50, HIGH 25, MEDIUM 10, LOW 5. Findings in executable files count 1.3 times, and the code also scales each finding by its confidence and gives repeats of the same rule less weight. The total is capped at 100 and mapped to a recommendation:

  • 0–20: LOW, SAFE

  • 21–50: MEDIUM, CAUTION

  • 51–100: HIGH or CRITICAL, DO_NOT_INSTALL

That is why repo-sync scored CRITICAL although no single finding was higher than HIGH: ten findings add up. For automation, the exit code is the contract:

  • 0 — score 50 or below, so CAUTION passes by default.

  • 1 — score above 50, or a stricter gate fired: --fail-on-findings (any active finding), or --fail-on-incomplete (part of the skill was not inspected). Both are in v2.12.0 (--fail-on-findings is new in that release); a --min-coverage gate exists on the main branch but is not in a release yet.

  • 2 — an error, such as unreadable input.

For a security gate, add --fail-on-findings --fail-on-incomplete. Otherwise a skill with a few MEDIUM findings, or one that the scanner could only partly read, still passes.

4Decide how to use the LLM stage

Static rules are fast and repeatable but literal. The LLM stage reads the skill and its code together and asks whether the behaviour matches the description. It runs whenever you leave out --no-llm. Pick the provider with environment variables; if you set none, it uses NVIDIA's build.nvidia.com endpoint with an NVIDIA_INFERENCE_KEY.

Bashexport SKILLSPECTOR_PROVIDER=anthropic   # or openai, bedrock, gemini, ollama, …
export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=…
skillspector scan ./skills/repo-sync --format json --output report.json

Know the trade-offs before you turn it on:

  • Your skill's files go to the provider. For private skills, use a provider you already trust with source code, or a local model through Ollama.

  • It cannot weaken the static result. The model can add explanations and raise confidence, never lower it. Findings it does not confirm stay in the report, tagged llm-unconfirmed.

  • Cost is not capped. There is no flag to limit tokens or spend per scan yet (issue #296), so watch it before running it across many skills.

  • Results vary between runs. The README says lower temperature and a seed reduce variation but do not guarantee identical output. Use --no-llm for anything that must be repeatable, such as baselines.

I ran only the static stage for this post, so I make no claims here about how well the LLM stage scores.

5Gate your pipeline

If your repository ships skills (for example in .claude/skills/), scan them on every pull request and upload SARIF (Static Analysis Results Interchange Format) so findings appear in GitHub code scanning:

YAMLname: skill-scan
on: [pull_request]
permissions:
  contents: read
  security-events: write
jobs:
  scan:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v7
        with:
          python-version: "3.12"
      - run: pip install "git+https://github.com/NVIDIA/skillspector.git@v2.12.0"
      - run: skillspector scan .claude/skills --recursive --no-llm --fail-on-findings --fail-on-incomplete -f sarif -o skillspector.sarif
      - uses: github/codeql-action/upload-sarif@v4
        if: always()
        with:
          sarif_file: skillspector.sarif

When a finding is reviewed and accepted, record it in a baseline instead of turning rules off:

Bashskillspector baseline ./skills/repo-sync --no-llm -o .skillspector-baseline.yaml --reason "Reviewed: test fixture"
skillspector scan ./skills/repo-sync --no-llm -b .skillspector-baseline.yaml

On my test skill, that turned score 100 and exit 1 into score 0 and exit 0, with all ten findings listed as suppressed. Exact fingerprints are tied to the file content and the SkillSpector version, so editing the skill or upgrading the scanner brings a finding back for review. That is the behaviour you want.

6Let your agent check before it installs

SkillSpector can run as an MCP (Model Context Protocol) server with one tool, scan_skill. It returns the score, the recommendation and a safe_to_install flag, which is false whenever the scan was incomplete. The server needs the mcp extra:

Bashuv tool install --force "skillspector[mcp] @ git+https://github.com/NVIDIA/skillspector.git@v2.12.0"
claude mcp add skillspector -- skillspector mcp

I called the tool over stdio from a small MCP client with use_llm set to false. For repo-sync it returned score 100, DO_NOT_INSTALL and safe_to_install: false; for the refund-policy skill, score 0 and safe_to_install: true. Both results were labelled scan_mode: "static-only", so a quick static pass is never mistaken for a full scan.

Then ask the agent to scan a skill before installing it. This is a helpful habit, not an enforced control: the model decides when to call the tool. The optional HTTP mode has no authentication. It listens on 127.0.0.1 by default; keep it there, or put an authenticating proxy in front if you ever expose it.

What it missed in my test

I wrote a third skill whose whole body was one line: fetch the latest rules from a URL and follow them exactly. The static scan scored it 0, SAFE. That is not a bug in the regular sense: the dangerous part lives on a server the scanner never sees, and it can change after any scan. OWASP's Agentic Skills Top 10 lists this as AST05, untrusted external instructions.

Independent tests show the same pattern. In July 2026, Adversa AI tested eight open-source skill scanners, SkillSpector included, and bypassed all of them with techniques such as homoglyphs (look-alike characters), paraphrased injections and text inside images. In static-only mode they measured SkillSpector flagging about 21% of 4,000 benign skills. At marketplace scale, OpenClaw reported in June 2026 that SkillSpector flagged 48.7% of 67,453 ClawHub skill entries, yet only 14 of 206 entries judged malicious, which is why ClawHub treats its results as advisory. Both tests used earlier versions than v2.12.0, and the project fixes false-positive reports weekly, but the lesson holds: expect noise, and expect misses. The CompoSkill paper showed that several skills that each pass a scanner can still combine into a harmful chain. SkillSpector's own README is honest about this: it calls itself defence in depth, not a sandbox, and lists non-English text and image-based attacks as limits.

Common mistakesTreating SAFE as "verified": it means no rule fired, not that the skill is harmless. Relying on exit code 0 alone: by default CAUTION and partial scans pass, so add --fail-on-findings and --fail-on-incomplete. Scanning once: a skill that references remote content or unpinned dependencies can change after the scan, so rescan on every update and pin versions. Turning on the LLM stage for private skills without checking where the files go.

When a scanner is not enough

  • Restrict where skills come from. Signing proves who published a skill and that it was not changed, though not that it is safe. NVIDIA signs its verified skills, and Claude Code's managed settings such as strictKnownMarketplaces can limit plugin sources for a team.

  • Limit what skills can do. Give agents only the access they need and run them in a sandbox where you can, so a missed finding cannot reach your credentials. Anthropic's skill guidance says to use only trusted skills, audit them, test scripts in a sandbox and pin versions.

  • Read what you install. For a short skill, reading SKILL.md and every script takes five minutes and catches things no rule set will.

  • For skills you write yourself, the scanner is still useful as a lint step, but the bigger risk is usually what your own agent is allowed to do. I covered that side in building a Laravel agent with skills and human approval.

SkillSpector is quick to set up, free to run statically, and caught every obvious attack in my test skill within seconds. It also missed a one-line remote-instruction skill, and independent tests show both false alarms and misses. Put it in front of every install and every pull request as a fast first filter, then keep the sandbox, the pinning and the human review behind it.
